abstract: Bacterial cell division depends on the tubulin homolog FtsZ, which assembles into a membrane-bound cytokinetic Z-ring. FtsZ filaments treadmill, growing at one end and shrinking at the other, and many regulatory proteins control where and when the Z-ring forms. Whether treadmilling itself confers a regulatory advantage, and how inhibitors exploit it, has remained unclear. Here we show that the Escherichia coli nucleoid occlusion factor SlmA caps the growing ends of treadmilling FtsZ filaments, converting steady-state subunit turnover into net filament shrinkage. Using in vitro reconstitution of membrane-bound FtsZ filaments with quantitative fluorescence and single-molecule imaging, we find that SlmA shortens filaments and reduces polymer mass at concentrations far below that of FtsZ, behaving like the bona fide capper FtsZ L272E. Structural prediction and mutagenesis identify a previously unrecognized interface between SlmA and the polymerization-competent surface of FtsZ that is required for activity in vitro and in vivo and that acts together with the known FtsZ C-terminal peptide contact. A minimal stochastic model shows why end capping outperforms sequestration and severing, establishing kinetic asymmetry as a general point of control for treadmilling cytoskeletal polymers.
